cues.text: Lecture two starts with a question. With so many new technologies, why learn nano?
The answer is convergent science and technology. Almost every new field falls under four areas.
Nano works with atoms. Bio, with genes and cells. Info, with bits. And cogno, with neurons.
Together, they aim at one goal: enhancing human performance. Nanomedicine, for example, combines several of them.
Nano is not a material. It is a mathematical prefix, like kilo or milli.
It means ten to the minus nine: one billionth.
It comes from the Greek word nanos, which means dwarf.
It works with any unit: a nanometer, a nanosecond, a nanogram.
Remember the conversions. One nanometer is ten to the minus nine meters, ten to the minus three micrometers, and ten angstroms.
So one hundred nanometers is zero point one micrometers, or one thousand angstroms.
How small is that? Shrink the Earth ten million times, and you get a football.
Shrink the football a billion times, and you get a fullerene: a nanomaterial of zero point seven nanometers.
Nanomaterials are the size of proteins, DNA and viruses.
We cannot see or feel them, so we need tools such as electron microscopes and atomic force microscopes.
Now a definition he said he may ask: the difference between nanoscience and nanotechnology.
Nanoscience is the study at the nano-size level. It is theory, on paper or on a computer.

Nanotechnology is working atom by atom: creating functional materials, devices and systems, controlling matter at one to one hundred nanometers, and exploiting the new properties. It is practice, in the lab.
So in a multiple choice question, words like create, control or lab point to nanotechnology. The word study points to nanoscience.
Nano is not new. People used nanoparticles for colour long before anyone knew what they were: the Lycurgus cup, and medieval stained glass.
Gold nanoparticles look red, green or orange, depending on their size.
But a gold ring is always yellow.
That is the key message of the course. At the nano scale, size and shape change the properties of a material. He will not ask the numbers, only this idea.
Nanotechnology is used almost everywhere: medicine, energy, electronics, sensors, coatings and food.
Every technology grows along an S-curve. A slow start with no funding.
Rapid growth when investors arrive. And then saturation.
Textiles, railroads, cars and computers all followed it.
Nanotechnology is at the beginning of its rapid growth. So, as the lecturer said, it is not late to learn it. It is right on time.
